paragraphs.heading: How fast a reaction goes
paragraphs.text: A reaction rate is the speed of a chemical reaction. It is tied to how quickly a product's concentration rises, or a reactant's concentration drops, over each unit of time. Chemists find it by tracking those concentration changes as time passes. The rate always comes out as a positive number, and it is given in units of mol/(L⋅s).

paragraphs.heading: From years to fractions of a second
paragraphs.text: Rates differ enormously from one reaction to the next. Iron rusting in ordinary air is slow and can go on for many years, while cellulose burning in a fire is over in fractions of a second. Some reactions are simply quicker than others by their nature. For most reactions, the pace also slows down as the reaction goes on.

paragraphs.heading: One rate, whatever you measure
paragraphs.text: The ingredients of one reaction can be used up at different speeds. If A has a coefficient of 1 in the equation and B has a coefficient of 3, B disappears three times as fast as A. To get a single rate, each change is scaled by the reciprocal of that substance's stoichiometric number, its count in the equation. That way the rate is the same whichever reactant or product a chemist chooses to watch.

paragraphs.heading: A catch in the definition
paragraphs.text: This simple definition only works for one reaction in a closed system whose volume stays fixed. Concentration can shift for reasons that have nothing to do with chemistry. Pour plain water into a pot of salty water and the salt concentration falls, even though nothing has reacted.

paragraphs.heading: What speeds it up
paragraphs.text: Many things change a reaction's rate, among them the kind of reaction, concentration, pressure, temperature, the solvent, electromagnetic radiation, a catalyst, surface area and stirring. Raising the concentration of a reactant makes its particles collide more often, and the rate rises. For a gas, raising the pressure has the same effect, since it really amounts to raising the gas's concentration.

paragraphs.heading: The role of heat
paragraphs.text: Running a reaction hotter usually makes it faster, partly because particles collide more often. The bigger reason is that more of the colliding particles carry enough energy to react, called the activation energy, so more collisions succeed. The Arrhenius equation describes how temperature affects rate. Not every reaction obeys this pattern: some rates do not change with temperature, and some even fall as it rises.

paragraphs.heading: Why coal needs a match
paragraphs.text: Coal burns in a fireplace where oxygen is around, yet coal kept in storage at room temperature does not. At room temperature the reaction runs so slowly that it is negligible. The heat from a match lets it get going, and after that the reaction warms itself because it releases heat. Other fuels, such as methane, butane and hydrogen, behave the same way.
